data.content_ref: inline:The mechanism conflates two conceptually distinct Popperian properties: corroboration (a historical measure of how a theory has survived past severe tests) and empirical content (a fixed logical property measuring a theory's falsifiability). The mechanism states 'We choose the better-corroborated theory because it has survived the most severe tests (highest empirical content),' parenthetically equating survival under testing with high empirical content. But in Popper's framework, empirical content is invariant through testing—it is determined by what the theory logically rules out, not by its track record. A well-corroborated theory can have lower empirical content than a less-corroborated or even falsified rival. By grounding the preference in 'highest empirical content,' the mechanism fails to justify why better-corroborated theories specifically (rather than merely more falsifiable ones) should be preferred. Additionally, the mechanism's final sentence is circular: it asserts 'the reason this holds is that Popper's preference... is defensible on his own terms... which is what the mechanism above establishes'—restating the claim as its own justification.
